name: Muhammad
role: Prophet of Islam; founder and ruler of the Medinan state (c. 571-632)
summary: Muhammad proclaimed the Quran as divine revelation and led the community in Medina as religious teacher, lawgiver, judge and military commander. His recorded positions combine religious law, mutual defence and welfare duties such as zakat with a ban on interest. He ruled through a covenant that included Jewish tribes as allies, and later expelled or fought some of them.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Watt (Muhammad at Medina, pp. 231-232 and the list of expeditions) records the forces he raised and led or sent out from Medina, from the first raids and Badr onward.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Quran 4:4 and 4:20-21 require a dower and treat marriage as a contract with legal rights, and 4:12 gives spouses inheritance.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: He hired a guide for the emigration to Medina (Bukhari 2263) and paid his cuppers in wages or food (Bukhari 2278), taking hired labour as normal.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: He paid the man who cupped him his wages, and Ibn 'Abbas adds that he would not have paid them had it been disliked (Bukhari 2279).

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Bukhari 3318 reports a woman entering Hell over a cat she tied and starved.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Quran 6:142-144 permits livestock for food; Muslim 5055 (in this edition) reports him saying to slaughter in a good way, sharpen the knife and let the animal die comfortably.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: At the taking of Mecca he ordered 'Abdullah b. Sa'd killed because he had been a Muslim and apostatized, and granted him immunity only reluctantly when 'Uthman pleaded for him (Ibn Ishaq, p. 550).

arms-reduction.rationale: Quran 8:60 tells believers to prepare all the power and steeds of war they are able, not to reduce arms.

assisted-dying.rationale: He told of a man who, impatient with the pain of a wound, cut his hand until he died, and of God forbidding him Paradise for hastening his death (Bukhari 3463).

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Quran 6:142-144 lists cattle, sheep, goats and camels as lawful for food and 5:1 declares livestock lawful; he sanctioned slaughter of cattle rather than banning it.

ban-interest.rationale: Quran 2:275 says God has permitted trade and forbidden interest, and in the Farewell Sermon he declared 'all usury is abolished', starting with that owed to his uncle al-'Abbas (Ibn Ishaq, p. 651).

ban-spanking.rationale: He said to command children to pray at seven and to beat them for it at ten (Abu Dawud 495).

character-from-environment.rationale: He said every child is born with the true faith and its parents make it Jewish, Christian or Magian (Bukhari 1385): an innate nature that upbringing can change, so low.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Contested: Quran praises private giving (2:261), yet 9:103 and 9:60 set a collected, officially administered zakat for the poor.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: He disapproved of the killing of a woman found dead after a raid, condemning the killing of women and children (Bukhari 3014), yet said of night raids that might hit them 'they are from them' (Bukhari 3012), so low.

civilizational-union.rationale: His covenant joined the believers of Quraysh and of the Medinan clans, of different tribes, into one political community bound to make war and peace together (Ibn Ishaq, pp. 231-232).

collective-defense.rationale: His covenant bound its parties to 'help one another against any attack on Yathrib' and each to help the other 'against anyone who attacks the people of this document' (Ibn Ishaq, p. 233).

conscription.rationale: When three Muslims stayed behind from the Tabuk expedition without excuse, he forbade all Muslims to speak to them (Bukhari 4418), sanctioning those who did not answer his call to arms.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Contested: Quran 42:38 and 3:159 call for consultation, and allegiance pledges were taken from followers, but his authority rested on his claim of divine commission (4:59).

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Quran 102:1 says competition in worldly increase diverts people, and 57:20 calls worldly life rivalry in wealth and children; 9:34 warns hoarders.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Quran 7:80-81 condemns men approaching men; 4:16 prescribes punishment for "the two who commit it" without naming the penalty and its reference is debated. No clear legal penalty in the Quran.

death-penalty.rationale: He ordered a married man who confessed to adultery stoned to death (Bukhari 6815) and had the men of 'Ukl who killed his herdsman put to death (Bukhari 6802).

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: He sent Mu'adh to Yemen with orders that zakat be taken from the wealthy and given to the poor (Bukhari 1395): a standing levy for the poor, not one to be cut.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Quran 2:190 and 22:39 permit fighting those who fight or wrong the believers, and 9:38-39 rebukes those who do not go forth when called; an obligation on every Muslim is stated only for mobilisations he called.

destroy-worshipped-objects.rationale: On entering Mecca at its conquest he struck the 360 idols around the Ka'ba with a stick, saying 'Truth has come and Falsehood will neither start nor reappear' (Bukhari 4287).

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Quran 4:34 says men are in charge of women and must maintain them, and 4:11 and 2:282 give women different inheritance shares and testimony weight; the Farewell Sermon sets out separate rights and duties of husbands and wives (Ibn Ishaq, p. 651).

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Quran 12:40: "Legislation is not but for Allah"; 4:59 ties obedience to those in authority to obedience to Allah and the Messenger.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: Quran 49:13 says peoples and tribes were made to know one another and the noblest is the most righteous, though 3:110 calls the believers the best community raised for mankind, so low.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: His covenant at Medina was a standing defensive alliance binding Muslims and Jewish clans to help one another against any attack (Ibn Ishaq, p. 233).

equal-conscription.rationale: When 'A'isha asked to take part in jihad, he told her 'Your Jihad is the performance of Hajj' (Bukhari 2875): the duty to fight fell on men.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Quran 49:13 says the noblest before God is the most righteous, and the Farewell Sermon says every Muslim is a Muslim's brother (Ibn Ishaq, p. 651); law still differed by sex, faith and free or slave status, so low.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Quran 43:32 states God raised some above others in livelihood and rank; 4:32 tells people not to covet what others have been given.

filial-duty.rationale: Quran 17:23: parents are to be treated well, never rebuked, even in old age; also 31:14 and 46:15.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Watt (Muhammad at Medina, pp. 231-232) records that every expedition was led by Muhammad or an Emigrant he appointed, and that a fifth of all spoils went to him as head of the umma. There was no legislature to compare with, so low.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Bukhari 2335: "He who cultivates land that does not belong to anybody is more rightful to own it."

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: Anas reported him saying that no time will come but the time following it will be worse (Bukhari 7068); the decline runs from his own age, not an ancient golden age, so low.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: He slaughtered two rams with his own hands as sacrifices (Bukhari 5558).

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Quran 2:221 forbids marrying polytheists, while 5:5 permits marrying chaste women of the People of the Book; marriage across religions is partly restricted.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: He ordered that an unmarried person guilty of fornication be flogged a hundred stripes (Bukhari 6831), the penalty the Quran sets, and judged by revealed rulings.

leader-cult.rationale: Bukhari 3445 reports him saying "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians praised the son of Mary, for I am only a Slave"; Quran 18:110: "I am only a man like you".

legalize-drugs.rationale: He had a drunk man beaten with palm-leaf stalks and shoes (Bukhari 6773), punishing intoxication as an offence.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Quran 24:2 and 17:32 prohibit sex outside marriage; Bukhari 2237 reports he forbade the earnings of prostitution; Quran 24:33 forbids compelling slave women into prostitution.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: No recorded position on sentencing repeat offenders; the fixed penalties in Quran 5:38 and 24:2 are about something nearby.

military-superiority.rationale: Quran 8:60 tells believers to prepare whatever force they can, to deter enemies.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: His covenant took the Jewish clans in as allies, 'one community with the believers' (Ibn Ishaq, p. 233), yet he later fought and expelled particular Jewish tribes for breaking their treaty (Bukhari 4028); his record points both ways.

more-religion-public.rationale: The covenant he issued at Medina founded the community on faith, the believers being 'one community (umma) to the exclusion of all men', and referred disputes to God and Muhammad (Ibn Ishaq, pp. 231-233).

national-mission.rationale: No recorded position on spreading a form of government; the call to spread the religion (Quran 3:110, 9:33) is about something nearby.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Quran 17:44 and 24:41 say all things in the heavens and earth glorify God, giving creation worth beyond human use; 55:10 says the earth was set down for creatures.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Quran 22:39 permits fighting by those attacked; Bukhari 2480 reports him saying whoever is killed protecting his property is a martyr. He endorsed defensive killing.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Quran 4:59 commands obedience to Allah, the Messenger and those in authority; Bukhari 7144 limits this only where orders involve disobedience to God.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Contested: Quran 2:236 and 2:229 let a husband divorce without a stated fault, but a wife's exit is conditional (2:229 on her giving up property).

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Quran 51:19 and 70:24-25 say the beggar and the deprived have a right in the wealth of the well-off; 17:26 commands giving relatives, the needy and the traveller their due.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: He was married to nine wives at once (Bukhari 5068).

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Of future rulers who would not follow his guidance, he said to listen to the ruler and obey 'even if your back is flogged and your wealth is snatched' (Muslim 4785 in this edition).

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Watt (Muhammad at Medina, pp. 230-234) describes pledges of war and of obedience made to him personally, and his demand that weak tribes seeking alliance promise to obey him; his authority also rested on prophethood, so low.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Quran 4:76 says believers fight in the cause of God and unbelievers in the cause of false gods, and 58:19-22 sets the party of Satan against the party of God.

population-transfer.rationale: He exiled the Banu al-Nadir after they broke their treaty and later exiled the Jews of Medina, Banu Qaynuqa among them (Bukhari 4028).

premarital-sex.rationale: He ordered unmarried people guilty of illicit intercourse flogged and exiled for a year (Bukhari 6831), and the Quran prescribes a hundred lashes for unmarried women and men alike.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: When prices shot up and people asked him to fix them, he refused: God fixes prices, and he wished no one to have a claim against him for an injustice in property (Abu Dawud 3451).

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: Asked twice to fix prices, he declined, saying he would pray instead and that it is God who makes prices low and high (Abu Dawud 3450).

priority-to-poor.rationale: Quran 9:60 lists the poor and needy first among zakat recipients and 59:7 says wealth should not circulate only among the rich.

property-fundamental.rationale: In the Farewell Sermon he declared his hearers' blood and property sacrosanct and said only what a brother gives willingly may be taken (Ibn Ishaq, p. 651); Quran 4:29 forbids consuming wealth unjustly. Zakat and the fifth of spoils (59:7, 8:41) qualify this.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Quran 59:7 gives state-held fai to orphans, the needy and travellers "so that it will not be a perpetual distribution among the rich"; zakat takes a share of private wealth for set recipients (9:60, 9:103).

punish-blasphemy.rationale: He had Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf killed for having 'hurt Allah and His Apostle' (Bukhari 4037) and ordered Ibn Khatal's singing-girls, who sang satires about him, killed (Ibn Ishaq, p. 551), yet his covenant let the Jewish clans keep their religion (p. 233): insult punished, other scriptural religions tolerated.

racial-pride.rationale: He said God had removed the pre-Islamic pride and boasting in ancestors and told people to stop boasting of their forefathers, since all are sons of Adam (Abu Dawud 5116).

reason-over-faith.rationale: Quran 2:3 praises belief in the unseen and revelation is the guide (4:59); the Quran also urges reflection, but faith in revelation is primary.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on general self-government, separate laws or no stated position, not on keeping a distinct economic system, and the statement now asks only whether a region joining a larger state should be free to keep its economic system.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Contested: Quran 42:13 and 21:25 say all messengers brought the same message of one God, but 3:85 rejects any way other than Islam.

religious-nation.rationale: His covenant made the believers one umma 'to the exclusion of all men', yet counted the Jews of B. 'Auf 'one community with the believers', each keeping its religion (Ibn Ishaq, pp. 232-233).

religious-offensive-war.rationale: On the Tabuk expedition he brought Christian Ayla and the towns of Jarba and Adhruh under his protection in return for poll tax, and sent Khalid to seize the Christian ruler of Duma (Ibn Ishaq, p. 607).

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Bukhari 7056 reports the allegiance he took required listening and obeying rulers unless one saw clear disbelief with proof from God; resisting a ruler merely for lawbreaking is not endorsed.

restrict-conversion.rationale: His order to kill the apostate 'Abdullah b. Sa'd (Ibn Ishaq, p. 550) bears on leaving Islam only, while conversion into Islam was sought, so low.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Divine descent is rejected: Quran 18:110 "I am only a man like you" and 112:3 "He neither begets nor is born"; Bukhari 3445 has him calling himself a slave of God.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Quran 4:82 says it has no discrepancy and he proclaimed it as the word of God; its literal reading is qualified by 3:7 on clear and allegorical verses.

separate-church-state.rationale: Under his covenant, disputes among the people of Medina were to be 'referred to God and to Muhammad the apostle of God' (Ibn Ishaq, pp. 232-233): the prophet was also the community's judge.

separated-powers.rationale: He came to combine judging disputes, command of the expeditions and the fifth of the spoils, though in his first years clan chiefs still limited his authority (Watt, Muhammad at Medina, pp. 228-232), so low.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Quran 30:30 refers to the fitrah on which God created people and says no change should be in the creation of Allah; 4:119 treats altering it as Satan's command.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Quran 4:34 says men are in charge of women and 2:228 gives men a degree over them; in the Farewell Sermon he allowed husbands to confine and beat, 'but not with severity', wives guilty of open unseemliness (Ibn Ishaq, p. 651).

simple-living.rationale: He told Ibn 'Umar to 'be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler' (Bukhari 6416), while Quran 7:32 asks who has forbidden the adornment and good things God brought forth, so low.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Quran 9:38-39 criticises those who hold back when called to fight; he expected obedience in his campaigns.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Quran 15:29 speaks of God breathing His spirit into the first human, and 2:201 asks for good in this world and in the Hereafter.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: As ruler he enforced religious morals by penalty, beating drunkards and flogging fornicators (Bukhari 6773, 6831).

suppress-opposition.rationale: Watt (Muhammad at Medina, pp. 228-229) records that he could not act directly against his Medinan opponent Ibn Ubayy, who was left unpunished, while at Mecca he ordered a few opponents killed even if found under the curtains of the Ka'ba (Ibn Ishaq, p. 550); the record points both ways.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Quran 9:60 limits zakat to listed categories, first the poor and the needy, rather than paying it to everyone.

taxation-theft.rationale: He made zakat a compulsory levy collected by his agents: Mu'adh was sent to take it from the wealthy of Yemen (Bukhari 1395), and Ibn Khatal was sent out to collect the poor tax (Ibn Ishaq, p. 550).

territorial-expansion.rationale: Under him Medina's rule spread to Mecca, Khaybar and, during the Tabuk expedition, to Ayla, Jarba and Adhruh, which paid him poll tax, while Duma's ruler was seized (Ibn Ishaq, pp. 515, 549-551, 607). Several campaigns answered attacks or treaty breaches, so low.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: At Khaybar he ordered al-Zubayr to 'torture him until you extract what he has' when Kinana b. al-Rabi' would not reveal the rest of a treasure (Ibn Ishaq, p. 515).

traditional-family.rationale: Quran 4:1 and 30:21 set marriage and kinship as the basis of the community; 17:23 on parents. He regulated marriage, dower and inheritance.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: His covenant let the Jewish clans keep their religion ('the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs') and bear their own expenses, and kept each clan's custom on blood-money (Ibn Ishaq, pp. 232-233); law was partly separate by community.

universal-morality.rationale: Quran 91:7-8 says the soul was inspired with its wickedness and righteousness and 30:30 points to a natural disposition; 7:157 speaks of commanding what is known as right.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Bukhari 7144 reports him saying a Muslim must obey the ruler unless ordered to disobey Allah, in which case one should not obey. Close but not the same as a law being void.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Contested: Quran 5:44 calls those who do not judge by revelation disbelievers, but Bukhari 7056 permits resistance only for clear disbelief, and Muslim reports obeying rulers who still pray.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: When the wife of Thabit b. Qays asked to leave him without blaming his character, he had her return the garden given as her dower and told Thabit to divorce her (Bukhari 5273).

women-must-cover.rationale: Quran 24:31 tells believing women to draw their head-coverings over their chests and 33:59 tells them to draw their outer garments over themselves; how much of the body is meant is disputed, so low.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Quran 4:7 and 4:11-12 give women an inheritance share, but generally half of a male relative's. A right to inherit exists; equality of that right does not, so contested.

women-suffrage.rationale: Told that the Persians had crowned Khosrau's daughter, he said 'Such people as ruled by a lady will never be successful' (Bukhari 4425), rejecting women's equal right to hold the highest office.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Distributing alms at the Farewell Pilgrimage, he told two robust men there was no share in it 'for a rich man or for one who is strong and able to earn' (Abu Dawud 1633).

notes: The Quran is treated as his proclaimed words; hadith (Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud) and Ibn Ishaq's biography are later reports (tier 4) and capped at medium. sunnah.com was unreachable (Cloudflare challenge), so hadith text comes from the fawazahmed0 hadith-api edition; Muslim numbers are that edition's. Later pass 2026-11-09 (claude-opus-5-5), bringing the audit to rules 5: Wikipedia sources (s2, s3, s6-s8) replaced by the texts they cite: the Covenant of Medina and the Farewell Sermon from Ibn Ishaq (Guillaume trans.), the record from Bukhari and from Watt, Muhammad at Medina (1956). Record over words: where the reports record his acts (executions, the assassination of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the expulsions, zakat collection, punishments for drinking and fornication, the order to kill an apostate at Mecca) the answer rests on them; Quranic verses answer only where no act is recorded. Themes searched in this pass: government (his powers in Medina, pledges, judging), world (Tabuk, Ayla treaty, Khaybar, alliances), economy (price fixing, wages, zakat, land), society (women in office and war, divorce, polygyny, children), and the candidate statements. Several verses and reports point in different directions on apostasy, blasphemy and war; those are answered 0 or low. Later jurists' rulings are not used. Modern institutions (parliaments, central banks, the UN, elections) have no counterpart in his record and stay null.
